finalResponse:
# Innovation Capacity & Experimentation Initiative
## Companion paper to the Employee Empowerment & Adaptive Culture Initiative — Recommendation for Sponsor Group

**Version 1.0 — for decision at the sponsor group meeting of 18 March, alongside Empowerment v2.0. For prior circulation to the fourteen regional people leads, the four regional MDs, and — new to this paper — the regional heads of product, operations and commercial. Not yet for employee communication.**

---

### How we would ask you to use this

Two notes, and then the substance.

**The first is a recommendation the sponsor group may not expect from us: this should probably not be a second programme.** It arrives as one because it was commissioned as one. But a region that receives two centrally-authored culture initiatives inside a single financial year will, quite reasonably, treat the second as evidence that the first was not serious. We have therefore built this on the same architecture, the same measurement spine and the same central-obligation protocol as the Empowerment paper, so that the sponsor group has the option of approving them as **one initiative with two workstreams and one name — chosen regionally**. Decision 1 in §12.5 is exactly that choice. We would not be disappointed to be overruled, but we would want the overruling to be deliberate.

**The second is the same courtesy we asked for last time.** The regional cards in §6 are working hypotheses, offered so that they can be corrected. Where a unit has its own diagnostic data, that data supersedes the card and the card is retired (§5.4 of the companion paper applies unchanged). A card returned unamended will be read not as agreement but as a sign that the conversation has not yet happened.

One addition on gates: §10 here is materially heavier than in the companion paper, because innovation programmes touch employee-invention statutes, IP assignment, competition law and regulated-market conduct in ways that behaviour programmes do not. Nothing in §3 or §7 should be described to an employee anywhere before §10 has been walked through with Group Legal, Group IP, the European Works Council secretariat and Group Reward.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Treat the variance between locations as a variance in *conditions*, not in *appetite*. Define four conditions centrally as floors — protected time, an answered route, pre-authorised risk capital, and retained credit — with an alternative-form process where a floor cannot lawfully be met. Devolve everything else: what counts as an idea, how it is voiced, who convenes, what it is called. Run four instrumented pilots in Year 1, deliberately different in design and identical in instrumentation. Bind the centre to a published response and reversal protocol. And ban idea-volume as a target before anyone thinks of it.**

| | |
|---|---|
| The reframe | Locations do not differ mainly in willingness to innovate. They differ in slack, in distance to someone who can say yes, in the personal cost of a visible failure, and in proximity to a customer whose problem is visible (§2) |
| Global mandate | **Four conditions only** (§3) — protected time; a route from idea to a dated answer; pre-authorised experiment capital; retained credit and attribution. Each a floor, each with a named-approver alternative-form route (§3.6) |
| Devolved to regions | Definition of "idea", forum design, cadence, language, whether contribution is individual or collective, recognition form, sponsor selection, and the programme's name |
| Year 1 shape | **Four pilots — one HQ-adjacent, one long-route (three or more layers from a yes), one deskless-majority, one recently-acquired entity** (§7) |
| Principal risk | Not employee reluctance. **Middle-manager delivery exposure** — innovation time comes out of a number someone is measured on (§8.2) |
| Second risk | Innovation theatre: rising idea counts, flat conversion, unchanged latency. Explicitly instrumented as a failure state (§8.5) |
| The centre's own obligation | **Published response protocol**: every routed idea receives a named human, a dated answer and a reason within 20 working days; central kill decisions are published with reasoning to the originating audience; response performance is reported quarterly beside regional metrics (§9) |
| Measurement | Behavioural proxies weighted 75%, survey items 25%. **Idea volume is a diagnostic, never a target** (§8.3) |
| Numeric failure test | Idea submissions +30% or more while funded-experiment conversion is flat and median idea-to-answer latency improves <15% = declared theatre, programme paused, no further capital (§8.5) |
| Investment sought | **$10.6M Year 1, $8.2M Year 2** (illustrative; assumptions §12.1), of which **$4.1M is experiment capital that must actually be spent** and $3.6M is time relief |
| Funding split | Central funds diagnostic, platform, instrumentation, central team, and **100% of experiment capital in Y1** (70% Y2, 40% Y3). Regions fund time relief with a 60% central offset in Y1, 30% in Y2, nil thereafter (§12.3) |
| Decisions requested | **Three** — §12.5, sought on **18 March** |
| Owner | Group Chief People Officer with the Group Chief Operating Officer as co-sponsor. We regard the second name as load-bearing (§12.6) |

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

Innovation output across a network tracks the **shortest available route to a yes**, the **recoverable cost of being wrong**, and the **quantity of uncommitted time**, far more closely than it tracks anything cultural. *(Considered practitioner assertion, drawn from our own past programmes and from the pattern in the commissioning brief — not a measured finding in this business. Evidence key at §14.)*

The observation that prompted this paper — "the level of proactive innovation varies significantly by location" — is almost certainly real and almost certainly mis-attributed. Before we accept that some of our offices are more inventive than others, we would want to rule out the duller explanation: that in some offices an idea reaches a decision in nine days and in others it reaches a decision in eleven weeks, or never, and that people have accurately learned which office they are in.

**The specific failure we are trying to avoid** is the one every large company has already run at least once: an idea portal, a hackathon, a poster campaign, and eighteen months later a database of 4,000 suggestions with no owner and a workforce that has learned not to bother. That outcome is worse than no initiative, because it burns the credibility a second attempt would need.

---

## 2. Diagnosis before we design

### 2.1 The framing we would gently ask the sponsor group to test

The brief describes a culture-and-creativity problem. The available evidence may describe a **routing, slack and downside-cost** problem. Only one of those responds to inspiration.

| Candidate driver of the location variance | What creativity training / campaigns do to it |
|---|---|
| No uncommitted time; every hour is booked to delivery | **Nothing.** The constraint is arithmetic, not attitudinal |
| Route to a decision is long, unnamed, or ends nowhere | Nothing until the route is built and answered (§3.2) |
| A failed experiment is personally career-costly | **Amplifies harm** — you have asked people to volunteer for exposure |
| No money can be spent without a business case that presumes the answer | Nothing — the gate kills the idea before it can be tested |
| Local P&L bears the cost, group bears the benefit | Nothing — the incentive wins every time (§8.2) |
| Ideas travel *to* HQ but never *from* the periphery | Worsens — confirms the periphery's read of its own standing (§11.3) |
| Working-language barrier suppresses half-formed thoughts | Nothing — needs channel design, not confidence (§11.1) |
| Customer contact concentrated in a few roles | Partially — but the real fix is contact redistribution (§11.2) |
| Genuine skills gap in framing and testing a hypothesis | **Improves** — this is the one case where training is the right instrument |

Exactly one row in that table is a training problem. We would like to know its weight before committing eight figures.

### 2.2 The diagnostic we propose

Six weeks, no design freeze until it reports.

| Component | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Route trace** | Take 25 real ideas already raised in the last 18 months across eight countries. Follow each one forward. Record: who received it, how long to first response, how long to a decision, what the decision was, whether the originator was told. This is the single most informative thing in the diagnostic and it costs almost nothing but persistence |
| **Slack audit** | In twelve units, measure committed vs uncommitted time at three levels. Not self-reported willingness — actual calendar and shift structure |
| **Downside interview** | 50 structured conversations on one question, asked several ways: *what has happened here to someone whose attempt did not work?* Confidentiality-protected, results reported without unit attribution below a threshold of 8 responses |
| **Spend-authority audit** | The smallest sum a named individual can commit to test something, without a business case, at each of four levels in each of eight countries. We expect this number to vary by two orders of magnitude across the network and to explain more than culture does |
| **Language and contact check** | Four sites where the working language is not the local one; plus mapping of which roles have direct customer contact |
| **Cost** | **$340K** |

If the route trace finds median idea-to-decision latency above six weeks anywhere, the Year 1 training envelope should be reduced and redirected to routing and spend authority before any commitment is made. That is the cheapest consequential decision available here.

### 2.3 The uncomfortable question, answered rather than deferred

*What does the centre give up?*

An innovation programme in which the centre keeps the right to absorb, re-badge, defund or silently ignore what the network produces is not an innovation programme. **§9 sets out four specific, testable, reportable central obligations** — a response service level, published kill reasoning, protection of experiment capital from in-year reallocation, and a reverse-adoption commitment. We would ask the sponsor group to adopt or amend §9, not to note it. If §9 is not adopted, our recommendation is to spend the $340K on the diagnostic, publish it, and stop there.

---

## 3. What is fixed everywhere: four conditions, stated as floors

Framed as conditions an employee is entitled to find in place, not as behaviours a manager must perform — so that very different local conduct can honour the same floor.

### 3.1 Condition I — protected time exists and is countable
**Floor:** every employee in scope can name a specific, recurring, protected allocation of time available for work not assigned to them, and can point to when they last used it.

The size is regional property. The floor is that it is **named, recurring and countable** — not "when you have a moment," which is the polite form of "never." For deskless and shift populations this will not be individual hours; the honouring forms are shift-overlap windows, rotation into an improvement cell, or a funded relief head (§11.2). For client-billable populations it must be reconciled with utilisation targets *before* launch, or the target quietly wins (§8.2).

**What this is not:** a mandated fixed percentage. We deliberately do not prescribe 15% or 20%. Imported percentages are the most-copied and least-transferable feature of other companies' innovation systems, and in most of our units they would be theatre by week three.

### 3.2 Condition II — there is a route from idea to a dated answer
**Floor:** every employee has at least one available route by which an idea reaches a person empowered to fund, kill or escalate it, and receives from that person **a decision, a date and a reason** within 20 working days.

The route form is entirely local: a written pre-read, a monthly forum, a shift huddle, a skip-level, a named broker role, a queue in the platform, a WhatsApp group with a rota. It need never be a pitch to a room. The **answered** part is the floor.

**The reason is not optional and not a formality.** "No, because we tried this in 2019 and here is what happened" keeps a contributor. "No" alone loses three more ideas that were never sent. Where an idea is killed, the reason is given to the originator and, at the originator's option, to the forum that saw it.

**Firewall, mandatory:** this route is expressly **not** the dissent channel of Empowerment Entitlement II, and expressly **not** any statutory reporting channel. Three separate things, separately named, separately routed, separately governed (§10.4).

### 3.3 Condition III — a bounded amount of risk capital is pre-authorised
**Floor:** in every unit, at least one named individual below the unit head can commit a defined sum to test an idea **without a business case and without an approval step**, within a published experiment perimeter (§3.7).

The sum is regional property and should differ by an order of magnitude between a 40-person branch and a 3,000-person operation. Our working suggestion is that it be large enough to buy a real test and small enough that losing it is unremarkable — in most units, somewhere between $5K and $25K per authorisation, with a quarterly cap.

**A null result is a completed deliverable.** An experiment that runs cleanly and disconfirms the hypothesis has done its job and is reported as done, not as failed. This is the sentence most likely to be nodded at and least likely to be believed, which is why §8.3 instruments it: the proportion of funded experiments with a *documented result of either sign* is a headline metric, and a unit reporting a 95% success rate is reporting that it is not experimenting.

### 3.4 Condition IV — the contributor stays attached
**Floor:** an idea that is adopted carries, in the record and in the telling, the name of the person or team that originated it; and the originator has a **right of first refusal** to be involved in taking it forward.

*Right of first refusal*, not obligation. Some contributors want the work; some want the credit and their existing job; some — in several regions, most — want the credit to attach to their team rather than to themselves. All three are honoured forms. What is not honoured is an idea arriving at the centre from a branch and re-emerging as a group initiative with no branch in it. That has happened in this company and people remember (§11.3).

**Statutory overlay:** in Germany and several other jurisdictions, employee inventions carry a *statutory* compensation entitlement that is not ours to design around, and attribution has legal as well as cultural weight (§10.2). Condition IV is drafted to sit above those floors, never below them.

### 3.5 Everything else is regional property
What counts as an idea. Whether contribution is framed individually or collectively. Forum design, cadence, symbolism, recognition form, whether recognition is public or private, sponsor selection, tooling, and the programme's name. **We would suggest the centre resist standardising even the name**, for the reasons given in the companion paper.

### 3.6 The alternative-form process

Identical in machinery to the companion paper, and deliberately so — one register, one approver, one review.

| Element | Provision |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Legal impossibility, collective-agreement conflict, regulatory prohibition, or structural impossibility. Not difficulty. Not cost. Not discomfort |
| Form | Two pages: which floor, why, the nearest form the unit *can* honour, and the condition under which the floor becomes reachable |
| Approver | **Group CPO**, countersigned by the Regional MD and by Group Legal; Group IP added where Condition IV is engaged |
| Duration | 12 months, renewable once with fresh reasoning |
| Visibility | Internally published register, shared with the empowerment register, reviewed quarterly by the sponsor group |
| Presumption | Accepted unless materially weaker than the floor. We expect **six to ten** in Year 1 — more than the companion paper, because the legal surface here is wider — and would be actively suspicious of zero |

### 3.7 The experiment perimeter (the thing that makes Condition III safe)

Pre-authorised capital without a perimeter is how a well-run company acquires a regulatory finding. Every unit publishes, before its first experiment, a one-page perimeter stating what may be tried without further approval. Our proposed default, to be adapted regionally:
